title: The Winning of a Queen: Chapter 5
paragraphs: _How King Arthur defeated the enemies of King Leodegrance, and how his royalty was proclaimed._

The next day, the Duke of North Umber and six fellow knights appeared on the field in front of the castle of Cameliard, just as he had promised that he and they would. The seven champions arrived in great style. Seven heralds rode in front of them with trumpets and tabards, and seven squires rode behind. Each squire carried the spear, the shield, the crest, and the small banner of the knight he served. The seven heralds blew their trumpets so loudly that the sound reached the farthest corners of Cameliard, and people came running from everywhere. While the heralds blew, the seven squires shouted and waved the spears and banners. The seven knights rode so proudly that those who watched them had hardly ever seen such a splendid show of chivalry.

They paraded up and down the field three times, from one end to the other. Meanwhile a great crowd, called there by the blowing of the heralds’ trumpets, stood on the walls and gazed down at the noble sight. All the Court of King Ryence came too, and stood on the plain in front of the King’s pavilion. They shouted and cheered for the Duke of North Umber and his six fellow knights.

Meanwhile King Leodegrance of Cameliard was so weighed down with trouble and shame that he would not show his face. He hid himself away from all his Court, and he would not let anyone come into his presence that day.

Even so, the Lady Guinevere went to him with several of her damsels. When the King refused to let her in, she spoke to him through the door and tried to cheer him, saying: “My lord King and father, I beg you to look up and take heart. I promise you that there is one who holds our cause in his hands, and he is truly a most glorious champion. He will surely come before this day is over, and when he comes, he will certainly overthrow our enemies.”

But King Leodegrance did not open the door. He said: “My daughter, you say that only to comfort me. In this time of trouble I have no help except God, with His good, strong help and grace.” And she said: “No, I am telling you the truth. The help that God sends you, He will certainly send through a worthy champion who at this very moment holds our cause in his hand.”
So spoke the Lady Guinevere. King Leodegrance still did not come out, but he was greatly comforted by what she had said to him.

So passed all that morning and part of the afternoon, and still no one came to answer the challenge the seven knights had declared. But while the sun was still three or four hours high, a cloud of dust suddenly appeared in the far distance. Out of that cloud came five knights, riding at great speed toward the castle. When they drew near the walls, the people saw that the knight riding first of all was the same White Champion who had earlier overthrown the Duke of North Umber. They also saw that the four knights riding with him were very famous, with great skill and glory in arms. They were Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Geraint, and Sir Pellias. The people of the castle and the town knew those four knights, because they had stayed two days at Cameliard. They were so famous that folk crowded in from far and near to look at them whenever they walked abroad.

When the people on the walls saw who those knights were, and saw the White Champion who had earlier brought them such great honor, they shouted aloud a second time, with a voice mightier than the first.

King Leodegrance heard the people shouting, and hope suddenly woke within him. He came out at once, as fast as he could, to see what was happening. There he saw those five noble champions about to enter the field below the castle walls.

The Lady Guinevere also heard the shouting and came out as well. And behold, there was the White Champion with those four other knights. When she saw the White Knight and his four companions-at-arms, her heart nearly broke with pure joy and gladness. She wept from the strength of her feeling, and laughed while she wept. She waved her kerchief to those five noble lords and kissed her hand to them, and the five knights saluted her as they rode past her and into the field.

When the Duke of North Umber learned that five knights had come to answer the challenge against him and his companions, he came out of his pavilion at once and mounted his horse. His fellow knights came out and mounted their horses too, and he and they rode out to meet those who had come against them.

When the Duke of North Umber came close enough, he saw that the chief of the five knights was the White Champion who had earlier overthrown him. So he said to the White Champion: “Sir Knight, once before I lowered myself to fight you, though you were unknown to me and to everyone else here. I did not ask who you were. I rode a course against you, and by the chance of arms you overthrew me. This quarrel is more serious than that. So I and my companions-at-arms will not ride a course with you and your companions, and we will not fight you, until I first know the rank of the man I am fighting. I ask you now to declare who you are and what your standing is.”

Then Sir Gawaine opened the visor of his helmet and said: “Sir Knight, look at my face, and know that I am Gawaine, the son of King Lot. So you can see that my rank and standing are even better than your own. Now I tell you that the White Knight yonder is of such a rank that he lowers himself when he fights you, and you do not lower yourself by fighting him.”

“Ho, Sir Gawaine!” said the Duke of Umber. “That is a very strange thing to say, for there are few in this world so exalted that they would lower themselves to fight me. Nevertheless, since you vouch for him, I cannot deny what you say. Yet there is another reason why we cannot fight you. Look, we are seven well-proven and famous knights, and you are only five. Consider how unequal our forces are, and that you are in great danger in taking on so dangerous a fight.”

Sir Gawaine gave the Duke of North Umber a very grim smile. “Many thanks for your pity, Sir Duke, and for the tenderness you show for our safety,” he said. “But you may leave that matter to us and rest easy about it. I think the danger you seven are in is every bit as great as ours. Besides, if you were not a belted knight, a simple man might suppose you were more careful of your own safety in this matter than of ours.”

At these words the face of the Duke of North Umber turned completely red. He knew that he truly had no great wish for this battle, and he was ashamed of what Sir Gawaine had said to him. Each knight closed his helmet and all turned their horses. One party rode to one end of the field and the other party to the other end, and there each took its place.

They arranged themselves like this. In the middle was King Arthur, with two knights on either side. In the middle of the other party was the Duke of North Umber, with three knights on either side. When they had lined up, they readied their spears and shields and made themselves fully prepared for the charge. Then King Arthur and Duke Mordaunt each shouted aloud, and the two parties hurled themselves at each other with such violence that the ground shook and thundered under the horses’ hoofs, and clouds of dust rose up toward the heavens.
They met in the middle of the field with an uproar so dreadful that the crash of it could be heard more than a mile away.
When the two parties had passed each other and the dust of the clash had risen, behold, three of the seven had been overthrown, and not one of the five had lost his seat.

One of those who had been overthrown was Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, and he never rose from the ground where he lay. King Arthur had aimed his spear straight into the middle of his defenses, and the spear had held. Its point had pierced the Duke’s shield and his body armor, and the stroke was so violent that the Duke was lifted completely out of his saddle and thrown a full spear’s length behind his horse’s rump. So died that wicked man. As King Arthur rode past him, the evil soul of the Duke left his body with a faint noise like the squeak of a bat, and the world was well rid of him.

When King Arthur turned at the end of the course, he saw that only four knights were left on their horses out of all the seven he and his companions had charged. He raised his spear, drew rein on his horse, and spoke to his knights like this: “Messires, I am weary of all this noise and quarreling, and I do not care to fight any more today. So go at once and attack those knights. As for me, I will wait here and watch your adventure.”
“Lord,” they said, “we will do our best, as you command.”

So those four good knights did as he commanded. They rode straight against the other four, much encouraged that their King was watching their effort. King Arthur sat with the butt of his spear resting on his instep, and looked over the field with great calm and a steady face.

The four knights who remained of the Duke of North Umber’s party did not come out to this second clash as readily as they had before. They now knew how great the skill of the other knights was, and they saw that their enemies were coming at them very fiercely, with great courage and eagerness. So their hearts melted within them with doubt and worry about how this second clash would end.
Even so, they prepared themselves with what resolve they could find, and came forward as they were called to do.

Then Sir Gawaine rode straight at the foremost knight, a well-known champion named Sir Dinador of Montcalm. When he came close enough, he rose in his stirrups and struck Sir Dinador such a fierce blow that it split the knight’s shield in two and split his helmet as well. Part of the blade of Gawaine’s sword broke off and stayed in the helmet.

When Sir Dinador felt that blow, his brains swam like water, and he had to grab the horn of his saddle to keep from falling off. A great terror fell upon him, and he swerved his horse violently to one side. He fled from that place with the terror of death hanging over him like a black cloud of smoke. When his companions saw the stroke Sir Gawaine had dealt, and saw Sir Dinador flee from him, they also swerved to one side and fled at top speed, full of terror at their enemies. Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Geraint, and Sir Pellias chased them as they fled. They chased them straight through the Court of King Ryence, and the knights and nobles of that Court scattered this way and that like chaff as they came. They chased the fleeing knights in among the pavilions of King Ryence’s Court, and no man stopped them. When they had driven those knights completely away, they returned to the place where King Arthur still held his post, steadily waiting for them.

When the people of Cameliard saw their enemies overthrown, and saw them flee from their champions, they shouted with all their might and made a great cheer. They did not hold back their loud shouting when the four knights came back from chasing their enemies and rejoined the White Champion. They cheered even more when the five knights rode across the drawbridge and through the gateway into the town.
So ended the great combat, one of the most famous in all the history of chivalry in King Arthur’s Court.

When King Arthur had accomplished his purpose and come back into the town, he went to the merchant from whom he had borrowed the armor he wore, and gave the armor back to him. He said, “Tomorrow, Sir Merchant, I will send you two bags of gold for the rent of the armor you let me have.”
The merchant said: “Lord, there is no need to pay me for that armor, for you have done great honor to Cameliard by your skill in arms.”
But King Arthur said: “Enough, Sir Merchant, and do not forbid what I say. Take what I shall send you.”
Then he went on his way, and, having put his cap of disguise on his head, he came back into the Lady Guinevere’s gardens.

When the next morning came, the people of Cameliard looked out and saw that King Ryence had gone away from before the castle completely. That night he had taken down his pavilions, withdrawn his Court, and left the place where he and his people had camped for the past five days. He had taken with him the body of the Duke of North Umber, carrying it away in a litter surrounded by many lighted candles and borne with unusual pomp and ceremony. When the people of Cameliard saw that he was gone, they were overjoyed, and they made merry, shouting and singing and laughing. They did not know how deeply angry King Ryence was with them, for his old hatred of King Leodegrance was only a small flame compared with the anger that now possessed him.
That morning Lady Guinevere walked into her garden, and with her walked Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine. There she saw the gardener’s boy again.
Then she laughed aloud and said to the two knights, “Messires, look! There is the gardener’s boy, who wears his cap all the time because he has an ugly spot on his head.”

The two knights knew who that gardener’s boy was, and they were greatly embarrassed by her words, and did not know what to say or where to look. Sir Gawaine spoke aside to Sir Ewaine, saying: “By Heaven, that lady does not know what kind of man the gardener’s boy is yonder. If she did, she would be more careful of her words.”

The Lady Guinevere heard that Sir Gawaine was speaking, but she did not hear his words. So she turned to Sir Gawaine and said: “Sir Gawaine, perhaps it offends you that the gardener’s boy wears his cap in front of us. Maybe you will go and take it off his head, as you offered to do two or three days ago.”
And Sir Gawaine said: “Peace, Lady! You do not know what you are saying. Yonder gardener’s boy could more easily take my head off my shoulders than I could take his cap off his head.”
At this the Lady Guinevere laughed openly, but in her heart she secretly thought about that saying and wondered greatly what Sir Gawaine meant by it.

Around noon that day, a herald arrived from King Ryence of North Wales. He walked in boldly before King Leodegrance, who was sitting in his hall with a number of his people around him. The herald said: “My lord King, my master, King Ryence of North Wales, is greatly displeased with you. You sent certain knights against Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, and those knights killed that excellent nobleman, who was a close relative of King Ryence. Also, you have given no answer to the demands my master has made for certain lands and castles bordering North Wales to be handed over to him. For these reasons my master is insulted beyond measure. King Ryence orders me to give you two conditions, and they are these. First, you must immediately hand over to him the White Knight who killed the Duke of North Umber. Second, you must promise at once that those lands will be handed over to King Ryence immediately.”

Then King Leodegrance rose from his seat and spoke to the herald with great dignity. “Sir Herald,” he said, “the demands King Ryence makes of me are the height of insolence. The Duke of North Umber died because of his own pride and foolishness. I would not hand that White Knight over to your master even if I were able to. As for the lands your master demands, you may tell King Ryence that I will not give him so much as a single blade of grass, or a single grain of corn that grows there.”

The herald said: “If that is your answer, King Leodegrance, then I am ordered to tell you this. My master, King Ryence of North Wales, will soon come here with a great army, and he will take by force the things you will not give him peacefully.” With those words he left and went on his way.

After the herald had gone, King Leodegrance went into his private room. There he secretly sent for the Lady Guinevere, and she came to him. King Leodegrance said to her: “My daughter, a knight dressed all in white, with no crest or emblem of any kind, has come to our rescue twice and defeated our enemies. Everyone says that this knight is your own special champion. I also hear that he wore your necklace as a favor when he first went out against the Duke of North Umber. Now I beg you, daughter, tell me who the White Champion is, and where he can be found.”
Then the Lady Guinevere was overcome with confusion, and she looked away from her father’s face. She said: “Truly, my Lord, I do not know who that knight may be.”

Then King Leodegrance spoke very seriously to the Lady Guinevere. He took her by the hand and said: “My daughter, you are now old enough to think about marrying a man who will cherish you and protect you from your enemies. Look, I am growing old, and I cannot hope to defend you always from the dangers that surround people of our rank. Also, King Arthur (who is a very great King indeed) has brought peace to this realm. Because of that, all the noble court of knights that once gathered around me has scattered to other places, where greater adventures can be found than in my peaceful kingdom. So, as everyone has seen this past week, I now have not one single knight I can depend on to defend us in times of danger like these that now threaten us. It seems to me, my daughter, that you could not hope to find anyone who could protect you as well as this White Knight. He truly seems to be a champion of extraordinary skill and strength. So it would be good if you felt yourself drawn to him, as he seems to be drawn to you.”

Then the Lady Guinevere turned bright red, as if with fire, all the way down to her throat. She laughed, even as the tears overflowed her eyes and ran down her cheeks. So she wept, and yet laughed as she wept. She said to King Leodegrance: “My Lord and father, if I give my affection to anyone in the way you speak of, I will give it only to the poor gardener’s boy who digs in my garden.”
At these words King Leodegrance’s face twisted with fierce anger, and he cried out: “Ha, Lady! Would you make a mock and a joke of my words?”

Then the Lady Guinevere said: “Indeed, my Lord! I am not joking and I am not mocking. I tell you truly that the same gardener’s boy knows more about the White Champion than anybody else in the whole world.” Then King Leodegrance said: “What is this you are telling me?” And the Lady Guinevere said: “Send for that gardener’s boy and you will find out.” And King Leodegrance said: “Truly, there is more in this than I can understand right now.”
The King summoned his head page, a boy named Dorisand, and told him: “Dorisand, go to the Lady Guinevere’s garden and fetch the gardener’s boy to me.”

So Dorisand the page went as King Leodegrance had commanded, and in a little while he came back, bringing the gardener’s boy with him. With them came Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Pellias and Sir Geraint. Those four lords stood near the door where they had entered, but the gardener’s boy came and stood beside the table where King Leodegrance sat. The King looked up at the gardener’s boy and said: “Ha! Would you wear your cap in our presence?”
Then the gardener’s boy said: “I cannot take off my cap.”
But the Lady Guinevere, who stood beside King Leodegrance’s chair, spoke up and said: “I beg you, Messire, take off your cap to my father.”
At this the gardener’s boy said: “At your request I will take it off.”

So he took the cap off his head, and King Leodegrance saw his face and knew him. When he saw who stood before him, he cried out loud in utter amazement. He said: “My Lord and my King! What is this!” Then he rose from his seat, went and knelt on the ground before King Arthur. He pressed the palms of his hands together and placed his hands between the hands of King Arthur, and King Arthur took King Leodegrance’s hands in his own. King Leodegrance said: “My Lord! My Lord! Is it really you who have done all these wonderful things?”
Then King Arthur said: “Yes. Whatever those things were, I did them.” He bent down and kissed King Leodegrance on the cheek, lifted him to his feet, and spoke kind words to cheer him.

Now the Lady Guinevere, when she saw what was happening, was astonished beyond measure. All at once she understood everything with amazing clarity. A great fear came over her, so that she trembled terribly, and she said to herself: “What things have I said to this great King, and how I have mocked him and joked about him in front of everyone around me!” At the thought of it, she pressed her hand to her side to calm the terrible pounding of her heart. So, while King Arthur and King Leodegrance exchanged royal greetings and compliments, she slipped away and stood by the window near the corner of the wall.
After a while King Arthur looked up and saw her standing far off. He went straight to her, took her by the hand, and said: “Lady, how are you?”

She said: “Lord, I am afraid of your greatness.” He said: “No, Lady. It is I who am afraid of you. Your kind regard means more to me than anything else in all the world. Otherwise I would not have served for these twelve days as a gardener’s boy in your garden, all for the sake of your good will.” She said: “You have my good will, Lord.” He said: “Do I have your good will in great measure?” And she said: “Yes, you have it in great measure.”
Then he bent his head and kissed her in front of everyone there, and so they were promised to each other.
King Leodegrance was filled with such great joy that he did not know how to contain himself.

After these events, there was a war with King Ryence of North Wales. Sir Kay and Sir Ulfius had gathered a great army, as King Arthur had ordered them to do. So when King Ryence attacked Cameliard, he was completely defeated and his army scattered. He himself was chased into his mountains like an outcast.

Then there was great rejoicing in Cameliard. After his victory, King Arthur stayed there for a while with a splendid Court of noble lords and beautiful ladies. There was feasting and jousting and many famous contests of arms, the like of which that country had never seen before. King Arthur and the Lady Guinevere were perfectly happy together.

One day King Arthur sat at a feast with King Leodegrance, and the two of them were in very high spirits. King Leodegrance said to King Arthur: “My Lord, what shall I offer you as a dowry with my daughter, when you take her away from me to be your Queen?”
Then King Arthur turned to Merlin, who stood near him, and said: “Ha, Merlin! What shall I ask of my friend as that dowry?”

Merlin said to him: “My lord King, your friend King Leodegrance has one thing which, if he gives it to you, will greatly increase the glory and fame of your reign, so that it will never be forgotten.”
King Arthur said: “I ask you, Merlin, tell me what that thing is.”
So Merlin said: “My lord King, I will tell you a story:

“In the days of your father, Uther-Pendragon, I had a certain table made for him in the shape of a ring, and so men called it the ROUND TABLE. This table had seats for fifty men, and the seats were meant for the fifty knights who were the most worthy in all the world. The seats were made in such a way that whenever a worthy knight appeared, his name showed in letters of gold on the seat that belonged to him. When that knight died, his name would suddenly vanish from the seat he had once held.

“Now, forty-nine of these seats were all alike, except for one that was set aside for the King himself. That one was raised higher than the other seats, and was skillfully carved and inlaid with ivory and gold. The fiftieth seat was different from all the others, and it was called the SEAT PERILOUS. It was unlike the others both in how it was made and in what it meant. It was skillfully set with gold and silver in curious designs, and it was covered with a canopy of satin embroidered with gold and silver. It was altogether wonderful and magnificent to look at. No name ever appeared on this seat, because only one knight in all the world could hope to sit there safely. If any other dared to sit in it, either he would die a sudden and violent death within three days, or some great misfortune would fall upon him. That is why the seat was called the SEAT PERILOUS.
“In the days of King Uther-Pendragon, thirty-seven knights sat at the ROUND TABLE. When King Uther-Pendragon died, he gave the ROUND TABLE to his friend, King Leodegrance of Cameliard.
“At the beginning of King Leodegrance’s reign, twenty-four knights sat at the ROUND TABLE.

“But times have changed since then. The glory of King Leodegrance’s reign has paled beside the glory of your reign, and his noble Court of knights has left him completely. So now not one name is left on any of the fifty seats around the ROUND TABLE, except the name of King Leodegrance. The ROUND TABLE now lies under its pavilion, entirely unused.

“Yet if King Leodegrance will give you, my lord King, that ROUND TABLE as a dowry with the Lady Guinevere, it will bring your reign its greatest glory. In your day every seat at that TABLE will be filled, even the SEAT PERILOUS, and the fame of the knights who sit at it will never be forgotten.”
“Ha!” said King Arthur. “That would indeed be a dowry worthy of any king to have with his queen.”

“Then,” King Leodegrance said, “you shall have that dowry with my daughter. If it brings you great glory, then your glory will be my glory, and your fame will be my fame. For if my glory fades and yours grows, look, is not my child your wife?”
King Arthur said: “You speak well and wisely.”

So King Arthur became the master of that famous ROUND TABLE. The ROUND TABLE was set up at Camelot (which some men now call Winchester). Before long there gathered around it such a company of knights as the world had never seen before that time, and will never see again.
That was the story of the beginning of the ROUND TABLE in King Arthur’s reign.
